extracted.intended_audience: law students, patent practitioners, policymakers, and interested members of the public seeking a summary of the Myriad decision and its implications for biotechnology patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and apply legal standards for whether genetic material or related claims (compositions, diagnostic methods, cDNA, drug screening assays) are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. §101, as interpreted by Myriad and related precedent. Focus is on U.S. Supreme Court and Federal Circuit rulings about products of nature, purified/isolated materials, and method claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter under §101
rubrics_metrics.description: "This part of U.S. law describes what is patent-eligible: 'any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof'. If the invention falls under one of several excluding categories, however, including a 'naturally occurring article' (a defined term in the law), then it is not patent eligible."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use §101 as the threshold inquiry for subject-matter eligibility. Identify whether the claimed subject falls within the statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter) and then determine if it is excluded as a product of nature or other non-eligible category. The Myriad decision applies §101 to genetic material claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product of nature doctrine / 'isolated' DNA not making it patent eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: "A naturally occurring DNA segment is a product of nature and not patent eligible merely because it has been isolated."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims to naturally occurring biological substances remain ineligible even if the claimed material is removed from its natural environment. Courts will ask whether the claimed material is merely an isolated form of something that exists in nature; mere isolation (or purification) typically is insufficient to confer patent eligibility under Myriad.

rubrics_metrics.name: cDNA patent eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court held that "cDNA is patent eligible because it is not naturally occurring" and that cDNA "should be patent eligible, because it does not exist in Nature but rather was 'engineered by man'."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complementary DNA (cDNA) — where introns are removed — can be treated as a human-made (non-naturally occurring) molecule for §101 purposes. Claims directed to cDNA are more likely to survive eligibility challenges, though scientific distinctions may be contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purified-and-isolated doctrine (historical standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO and courts historically allowed patents on molecules when 'isolated from their natural state and purified' (e.g., aspirin, adrenaline, vitamin B12, prostaglandins). Quoted USPTO guideline: 'Like other chemical compounds, DNA molecules are eligible for patents when isolated from their natural state and purified or when synthesized in a laboratory from chemical starting materials.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This older doctrine supported claims to isolated natural molecules; Myriad effectively narrowed or rejected its application to naturally occurring DNA sequences. When evaluating older claims or prior PTO practice, consider that purified-and-isolated reasoning may no longer control post-Myriad for genomic sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different test (Diamond v. Chakrabarty)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chakrabarty test asks whether the claimed subject is 'markedly different' from products found in nature (used in Federal Circuit reasoning to support patent eligibility of isolated DNA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may use a 'markedly different' analysis to ask whether the claimed composition possesses characteristics that make it significantly different from a natural counterpart. Applying Myriad, chemical/structural differences that make a molecule non-naturally occurring (e.g., cDNA, engineered organisms) support eligibility, but informational identity to a natural sequence may counsel against eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept requirement (Mayo framework applied to laws of nature/product of nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Mayo precedent, a claim involving a law of nature must have an 'inventive concept' that does 'significantly more than simply describe…natural relations.' The Court and dissent applied similar reasoning to products of nature: does the claimed composition involve enough inventiveness beyond the natural product?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For claims touching natural laws or natural products, examine whether the claim adds an inventive concept beyond conventional, well-understood, routine activity. If the claim merely states a natural law or a naturally occurring product without meaningful human-made alteration or application, it risks ineligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method/diagnostic claims as abstract mental processes (Bilski/Mayo)
rubrics_metrics.description: The District Court and Federal Circuit found that comparisons of DNA sequences were 'abstract mental processes' (In re Bilski) and therefore not patent eligible; the Court noted method claims that 'involve well-understood, routine, conventional activity previously engaged in by researchers' add nothing inventive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnostic or analysis method claims that essentially claim mental steps (e.g., comparing sequences, thinking about correlations) without a concrete, transformative step are vulnerable to §101 invalidation. Evaluate whether the claimed method effects a real-world transformation or merely recites an abstract practice or mental process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformative-step requirement for method claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims lacking transformative steps cover only patent-ineligible abstract, mental steps; the Federal Circuit held that method claims 'directed to
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods must include concrete, non-conventional steps that effect a transformation or application beyond abstract scientific principles. Mere instructions to compare or analyze data without inventive laboratory or technological steps will likely be treated as ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope distinction: composition of matter versus information
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit treated gene claims as directed toward 'compositions of matter' rather than toward information, but the Supreme Court emphasized that genes and the information they encode are not patent eligible under §101 simply because they have been isolated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting or evaluating claims, distinguish whether the claim is to a physical, human-made composition (more likely eligible) or to information/content (less likely eligible). Claims that are essentially to informational content (sequence as information) are more vulnerable under Myriad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of applications of knowledge about genes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court noted: 'This case does not involve patents on new applications of knowledge about the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes... Many of [Myriad's] unchallenged claims are limited to such applications.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that apply knowledge of a gene to new, specific, technological uses (diagnostic tools with inventive steps, therapeutics, engineered alterations) may be patentable even if the underlying natural sequence is not. Focus claims on concrete applications or methods that add inventive contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovative laboratory methods can be patentable (methods of isolation not implicated here)
rubrics_metrics.description: The opinion: 'Had Myriad created an innovative method of manipulating genes... it could possibly have sought a method patent.' The Court observed Myriad's isolation methods were 'well understood, widely used, and fairly uniform' and thus not at issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventive, non-routine laboratory processes for manipulating genetic material may be eligible as method patents. When the process itself provides innovation beyond routine isolation/ purification, draft claims to emphasize those novel process steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drug screening claims — mixed treatment in precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit found drug screening assay claims patentable, and the Supreme Court's decision did not broadly invalidate drug screening claims; prior to Myriad, drug screening claims were 'not seriously questioned.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drug-screening/assay claims that describe concrete experimental steps and applications are more likely to be treated as patent-eligible than claims that merely state a principle or observational correlation. Assess claim drafting to emphasize practical experimental implementations and inventive features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation and enforcement context (injunctions and §287(c) limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: The article notes Myriad continued litigation but could not obtain preliminary injunctions per eBay Inc. v. MercExchange, L.L.C., and cites 35 U.S.C. §287(c) ('This subsection (exemptions of patent infringement for doctors) does not apply to the activities of any person...who is engaged in ...the provision of ... clinical laboratory services').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond eligibility, consider enforceability remedies (injunctions) and statutory limitations/exemptions that affect how patents on biotech/diagnostic services are enforced. Eligibility invalidation is not the only litigation risk; procedural and statutory defenses can affect relief.
